spec_choices.why: The source allows 3 to 4 and the designer chose 4. Three is the smallest table with more than one opponent to set the contract against. More than 4 would exceed the 36-card pack's balance and make each trick too crowded for a 3-card hand to steer.
The rules forbid discussion; players communicate only through bids and cards.
A text code per card lets the engine check suits and ranks arithmetically.

spec_choices.what: Declarer tie-break done by updating on bid >= high_bid in bidding order

A thoughtful player bids from hand strength and from the bids already made, since bidding last wins ties. Opponents cooperate to break the contract, either by taking tricks from the declarer or by giving tricks away when the declarer bid low.

variation.original_summary: Rutersju is a Scandinavian trick-taking game for 3 to 12 players. Each player gets three cards from a 36-card pack and bids the exact number of tricks they will take. The highest bidder plays alone as declarer against everyone else, and the diamond 7 is a super-trump that wins any trick it is in. The declarer scores the bid if it is made exactly; otherwise every opponent scores one point per trick of miss.

review.evidence: The policies are not trivially dominant. Always bidding 3 makes you declarer often but rarely exact, and each miss feeds every opponent. Always bidding 0 rarely makes you declarer. There are seat problems, though. Ties go to the last tied bidder, and no rotation is stated, so a fixed last seat wins every tie. A made 0-bid scores 0, so when everyone bids 0 the contract is worthless to the declarer. With 12 players only 36 cards exist, so the whole pack is dealt and the diamond 7 is always in play. At 3 players it is in play only a quarter of the time.

Three-card hands make a single deal close to a lottery: whoever holds the diamond 7 or a long suit of honours decides it. The rules state no number of deals, so luck is never averaged out. Over many deals, careful bidding and defending do matter.

Exact bidding means a weak hand can still win a 0 or 1 contract. Defenders must cooperate silently to push the declarer off the exact count, either by feeding tricks or by stealing them. A strong player keeps finding better ways to read the bids and use the leads.

Hands are hidden. Bids, made in turn, signal hand strength. Card play reveals more information trick by trick. The defenders must infer one another's holdings without talking, and the declarer must plan three tricks ahead to land exactly on the count.
Trick winners follow from rank and suit. Scores are bid or bid difference, all arithmetic.

The game is turn-based text with hidden hands, which the platform supports. However, it has no fixed length or winner rule. The 12-player version makes rounds long. A trick's turn order changes with the trick winner, which needs explicit handling.

problems: No number of deals and no winner rule: a single 3-card deal is mostly luck, and the game never ends by arithmetic.
The tie rule (last tied bidder wins) hands a permanent edge to a fixed seat unless the bidding order rotates, and no rotation is stated.
A declarer who makes a 0 bid scores 0, so a 0 contract is worthless. When everyone bids 0, the last bidder is forced into a pointless contract.
Player counts up to 12 make rounds too long and exhaust the deck, which changes the game's character by player count.
Talk among the defenders would let them announce their cards (for example 'I hold the diamond 7'), which would remove the hidden-hand inference that drives the defence.

changes.what: Play exactly 12 deals. The highest total after 12 deals wins; a tie for the top is a draw.
changes.why: Gives the game an arithmetic end and averages hand luck over many deals, so bidding and defending skill decide the result.
changes.fixes: No number of deals and no winner rule: a single 3-card deal is mostly luck, and the game never ends by arithmetic.

changes.what: The first bidder rotates one seat clockwise each deal. 12 deals divides evenly by 3 and by 4, so every seat bids first, and last, equally often.
changes.why: The tie-goes-to-last advantage is shared equally among all seats.
changes.fixes: The tie rule (last tied bidder wins) hands a permanent edge to a fixed seat unless the bidding order rotates, and no rotation is stated.

changes.what: A declarer who takes exactly the bid scores the bid plus 1. Failure is unchanged: each opponent scores the number of tricks of difference.
changes.why: A 0 contract is now worth 1 point, so every contract has value. Failure still feeds every opponent, so a reckless high bid is punished.
changes.fixes: A declarer who makes a 0 bid scores 0, so a 0 contract is worthless. When everyone bids 0, the last bidder is forced into a pointless contract.

changes.what: Limit the game to 3 or 4 players. Keep the 36-card pack, so 9 or 12 cards are dealt and the rest stay unseen.
changes.why: Keeps each round short and inside the step limits. Leaves undealt cards, so nobody knows whether the diamond 7 is in play, which keeps inference alive.
changes.fixes: Player counts up to 12 make rounds too long and exhaust the deck, which changes the game's character by player count.

changes.what: No discussion phase. The only signals are bids and cards played.
changes.why: The defenders share an interest only against the declarer. Talk would let them reveal their hands outright, and the game's reasoning is inferring hands from bids and play.
changes.fixes: Talk among the defenders would let them announce their cards (for example 'I hold the diamond 7'), which would remove the hidden-hand inference that drives the defence.

keeps: 36-card French pack, three-card hands, three tricks per deal
The diamond 7 as the unbeatable card
Bids from 0 to 3 for an exact number of tricks, made in turn, with ties going to the last tied bidder
One declarer who leads first and plays alone against all the others
Must follow suit; the highest card of the led suit wins
Exact-or-fail scoring, with failure paying every opponent the size of the miss

recommendation.reason: The core (exact bidding, a lone declarer, silent cooperation among the defenders, hidden hands) rewards inference. It needs only a fixed length, seat rotation, a value for 0 contracts and a smaller player count.

variation.name: Rutersju Twelve
variation.summary: 3 or 4 players play 12 deals of three-card Rutersju. In each deal the highest bidder declares an exact trick count and plays alone against the rest, who try to push the declarer off the count. The highest total after 12 deals wins.
variation.rules:
CARDS. Use a 36-card pack with four suits (spades, hearts, diamonds, clubs). Each suit has the ranks A, K, Q, J, 10, 9, 8, 7, 6, from high to low. The diamond 7 is special: it wins any trick it is played to. Otherwise it is a diamond.

SEATS. Players sit in a fixed clockwise order, and every player starts at 0 points. The game lasts exactly 12 deals. In deal 1, seat 1 bids first. In each later deal, the first bidder is the next seat clockwise from the previous deal's first bidder.

EACH DEAL.
1. Deal. Shuffle all 36 cards and deal 3 cards face down to each player. Each player sees only their own hand. The remaining cards stay unseen for the whole deal.
2. Bid. Starting with the first bidder and going clockwise, each player in turn announces a bid of 0, 1, 2 or 3. All bids are public as soon as they are made. Every player must bid; there is no passing.
3. Declarer. The player with the highest bid becomes the declarer. If several players tie for the highest bid, the one of them who bid last becomes the declarer. The declarer's bid is the contract. All other players are opponents for this deal.
4. Play three tricks. The declarer leads the first trick. In each trick, the leader plays one card face up. Then each other player in clockwise order plays one card face up. A player who holds a card of the led suit must play a card of that suit. A player with none may play any card. If the diamond 7 is in the trick, its player wins the trick. Otherwise the highest card of the led suit wins. Each player's tricks are counted separately. The winner of a trick leads the next one. All played cards stay visible to everyone.
5. Score. Count the declarer's tricks.
   - If the declarer took exactly the contract, the declarer scores the contract plus 1 point. A contract of 0 made scores 1; a contract of 3 made scores 4.
   - If the declarer took more or fewer tricks than the contract, every opponent scores points equal to the difference between the contract and the declarer's tricks. The declarer scores nothing.
   - Opponents' own tricks are never scored.
6. Announce. Announce every player's total. Then start the next deal.

There is no discussion at any time. Players communicate only through their bids and the cards they play.

END. After the 12th deal is scored, the game ends.
variation.objective: After 12 deals, the player with the highest total points wins. If two or more players tie for the highest total, the game is a draw.
variation.expected_effect: Bidding becomes a contest of reading hands. A high bid wins the declarer seat, but a miss pays every rival. A bid also reveals strength, which the defenders use against you. The defenders must silently coordinate to make the declarer miss, by feeding unwanted tricks or taking needed ones, while still competing among themselves for the top total. Rotating the first bidder removes the seat edge. Twelve deals average out the luck of the diamond 7. The bid-plus-1 reward makes even a weak hand worth declaring at 0 or 1. Simple policies lose: always bidding 3 hands every opponent points almost every deal, and always bidding 0 forfeits the declarer seat to whoever reads the table. There is no talk, because the defenders' shared interest would let them simply reveal their cards.

balanced.evidence: Declarer payoff for contract c, where p is the chance of taking exactly c tricks: +(c+1) if made. If missed, the declarer gets 0 and every opponent gets |c - t|. Relative swing of declaring against each opponent = (c+1)p - (1-p)E|c-t|. Table, using rough 3-card estimates with opponents defending against the declarer: c=0 (needs 0 tricks while leading the first trick; only arises when everyone bid 0): +1 vs about -1.2, p roughly 0.3-0.5, about neutral or negative, so nobody wants it. c=1 with a typical hand: +2 vs -1.2, p about 0.4 gives 0.8 - 0.72, about 0; with a good hand (an ace or the diamond 7) p about 0.6 gives +0.7. c=2: +3 vs about -1.5, worthwhile only with 2 near-sure winners. c=3: +4 vs about -2, p is tiny without the diamond 7 and two aces, so strongly negative on average. Thoughtless policies under the WINNER RULE (highest total after 12 deals). (a) Always bid 3: declares whenever no later player bids 3, misses most contracts, and hands every opponent 1-3 points per miss, so it loses almost every game. (b) Always bid 0: almost never declares and earns only from other players' misses. Whenever a sensible declarer makes a contract, it falls behind by c+1, and sensible players declare only with positive edge, so it loses to sensible play. Against random bidders it does well, because random players overbid, but it is not a never-lose policy. In the all-0 case it is forced into the 0 contract when it bids last. (c) Always bid 1: about break-even EV, beaten by players who bid according to their hand. No bid is strictly better whatever the others do, because the value of each bid depends on hand strength and on the later bids. Seat edge: the last bidder sees all bids and wins ties. The first bidder rotates every deal, so with 12 deals each seat bids first 4 times (3 players) or 3 times (4 players), which removes the seat edge exactly. Opponents share an interest in the declarer missing, and the declarer role passes around, so every player can realistically win. The labelled payoffs match their description: contract 0 made scores 1, contract 3 made scores 4.

playable.evidence: The rules are complete: ranks and suits, the diamond 7 rule (it wins any trick, and when led it is a diamond lead that must be followed), follow suit, the trick winner leads next, the first bidder rotates, ties go to the last tied bidder, the forced 0 contract when all bid 0, absolute-difference scoring, and a tie on the final total is a draw. The game is finite (12 deals x 3 tricks), and the winner is decided by arithmetic on stored totals and per-player trick counters. Limits: steps 14 <= 20; choice steps 4 (one sequential bid round and three sequential tricks) <= 4; attributes 10 <= 20; hidden elements 1 (the hands) <= 3; random draws 1 (shuffle and deal) <= 1; rounds 12 <= 40. Engine fit: hidden_hands, sequential_choice and fixed_rounds are supported. The deal is a shared-deck draw handled through the workaround. The follow-suit legality check can be ruled by the referee. Nothing needs a board, a clock or trading. Talk: none, which is sensible here. Opponents share one aim, making the declarer miss, so open talk would mostly be one opponent proposing and the others copying. The real conflict, the bidding, already sends information through public bids. This is not a repeated cooperation game, so there is no case of a safe option winning every late round. In late deals, trailing players must take declaring risk, which adds planning rather than removing choice.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence: Chance is substantial: 3-card hands vary a lot, and the diamond 7 is a big swing. I estimate 40-55% of a single deal's outcome is chance, and over 12 deals the hands average out a fair amount. If everyone plays the intended strategy (bid your realistic exact trick count, defend to push the declarer off the contract), the winner is not fixed by the deal. Points come from exact contracts, and a weak hand can still bid low and earn as an opponent. Skill shows in several places. Estimating exact tricks matters, since overbidding gives points to every opponent. Bidding last lets a player infer others' hands from their public bids and decide whether to outbid. Card play involves ducking or overtaking so the declarer lands on a wrong count. Players can track the 36-card pack, with 27-28 cards unseen. Score position matters in the last deals. A player who models bids and defends well should clearly beat a random or overbidding player over 12 deals.

design_flags_left: the built game has 23 steps per round, over the limit of 20

triage.reason: The game plays only one trick per round. After round 1 every hand still holds 2 cards and trick_number is 1, and after round 2 deal_number is still 1, so a 12-deal game cannot fit the 12 rounds the rules imply. The tests rightly treat one round as one complete deal (deal, bid, three tricks, score), and the platform's counted repetition can express all three tricks inside one round.
triage.guidance: Make each round one whole deal. Increment deal_number and set first_bidder = ((deal_number-1) mod N)+1. Shuffle and deal hand_size cards to each player. Run the sequential bid poll starting from first_bidder. Set the declarer to the last of the highest bidders, and set contract and is_declarer. Then play tricks_per_deal tricks using counted repetition, not one trick per round: in each trick the leader plays first, then the others follow clockwise, following suit where possible. The 7 of diamonds wins any trick it is in, otherwise the highest card of the led suit wins, and the trick winner leads the next trick. Score at the end of the same round. By then every hand is empty, the deck holds 36 - 3N cards, and the round count equals deal_number, with deals = 12 as the fixed number of rounds. Reset bid, tricks and is_declarer at the start of each deal.

triage.reason: The game is built correctly, but the design has two flaws. It needs 23 steps per round, over the limit of 20. And a thoughtless policy (always bid lowest and play the first legal card) wins well over half its games, while always bidding high loses badly.
triage.guidance: Rebalance the bidding first. Right now a low bid is safe: you rarely become declarer, and when someone else overbids and fails, you score from their miss. A high bid makes you declarer, and with only 3 cards and hidden hands it often fails and hands points to everyone else. Possible changes: (1) Make high contracts pay much more when made, for example a made contract scores 2 x contract + 1, so a made 3 scores 7. (2) When a contract fails, the declarer loses the difference instead of every opponent gaining it, or only the opponent who took the most tricks gains. (3) If every bid is 0, nobody declares and nobody scores that deal, so an all-zero bid round earns nothing. Then cut steps to get under 20: drop the special diamond 7 (plain highest card of the led suit wins), and/or simplify play, for example a single bidding pass and a lower hand size or trick count. Keep the bid range matched to the trick count. After the change, check that neither the always-lowest nor the always-highest choice wins clearly more than its fair share against random seats.
